title: "A clear victory"
hookLine: the treaty is called a clear victory, and peace lets the call of Islam spread (48:1)

lines: DEARER THAN ALL THE SUN RISES ON.
cards: The pilgrims are riding home to Medina, heads shaved, no pilgrimage done, and the mood is heavy. Umar can't let it go. He rides up beside the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and asks him something, and gets no answer.
He asks again. Nothing. A third time.
Nothing. Umar drops back, sure he's gone too far, afraid a verse is about to come down about him. Then someone calls his name: the Prophet wants you.
Umar rides up, braced for the worst. And the Prophet says, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it: tonight a surah has come to me that is dearer to me than everything the sun rises on.

teach.b: The surah is al-Fath, the Victory, Surah 48. It opens: we have given you a clear victory, fathan mubina. Fath means an opening, and a victory, the same root as al-Fattah, the Opener, one of the names from a few weeks ago.
Umar, in another report, asks the obvious thing: messenger of God, is this a victory? And the Prophet says: yes. Everyone could see what had been lost.
The surah saw what had been opened. With the roads at peace, people could travel between Mecca and Medina without fear. They talked and traded.
Families on both sides met again. And they heard the Qur'an, not over the noise of war, but in ordinary conversation.

The early scholar az-Zuhri, as Ibn Ishaq reports him, said there was no greater victory in Islam before it: in the two years after Hudaybiyyah, as many people became Muslim as in all the years before, or more.
Ibn Hisham, who edited Ibn Ishaq's book, pointed to the numbers: about fourteen hundred came to Hudaybiyyah, and two years later, ten thousand marched to Mecca.
Two of Mecca's commanders, Khalid ibn al-Walid, the man who turned the battle at Uhud, and 'Amr ibn al-'As, came to Medina during the peace and became Muslim.
Even the clause that hurt most, sending back those who fled Mecca, was dropped by the Meccans themselves not long after, when it started to cost them more than it cost the Muslims.

teach.h: YOU MAY DISLIKE WHAT IS GOOD.
teach.b: The Qur'an says elsewhere that you may dislike something that is good for you.
Hudaybiyyah is often told to show what that line means.

how: Some Muslims recite Surah al-Fath in times of hope, and teachers point to Hudaybiyyah when counseling patience with setbacks and trust that a loss may be an opening.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the surah of victory came after a battle
it came on the way home from a treaty everyone thought was a loss.
Khalid ibn al-Walid became Muslim during the peace
he and 'Amr ibn al-'As both came to Medina in those years.
the Meccans later dropped the clause about sending people back
it started to cost them more than it cost the Muslims.

games.q: you're Umar, riding home from Hudaybiyyah. the Prophet tells you a surah has come calling this a clear victory. what do you ask?
o: nothing. you accept it at once.
messenger of God, is this a victory?
can we go back and fight?
games.why: he asked the obvious thing, and the Prophet answered: yes. what everyone saw lost, the surah saw opened.

practice: Bring back something from your past that felt like a clear loss at the time, a rejection, a breakup, a plan that fell apart, and stay with how it felt then.
Now look at what it opened, what came into your life through the gap it left; it may be nothing yet, and that's allowed. Just look, with Umar's question: is this a victory?

wordCard.voice: Fath, opening: what the Qur'an called the treaty everyone thought was a loss, the peace that opened the way.

orig.note: Arabic: a clear victory, a clear opening (48:1). fath shares a root with al-Fattah, the Opener.

carryVoice: Your line: losing, then winning. Some losses are too early to call. That's day two hundred seventy-four.

sources.ref: Qur'an 48:1 (we have given you a clear victory)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4177, 4833 (Umar's three questions; dearer than all the sun rises on)
Sahih Muslim 1785 (is it a victory? yes)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): az-Zuhri on the victory; Ibn Hisham's comparison of 1,400 and 10,000; the conversions of Khalid and 'Amr
Qur'an 2:216 (you may dislike a thing that is good for you)
